hypotheses.title: releaseManagedNFT require(true) never reverts on missing NFT
hypotheses.description: After the loop that searches for `nftContract` in `ManagedNFTs`, the code contains `require(true, "unable to find released NFT in ManagedNFTs");` which is a no-op. If the NFT was not found (e.g., already released or never added), the function still succeeds and emits `ReleaseManagedNFT`, leaving state inconsistent with the actual transfer.
hypotheses.attackPath: Not directly exploitable by an untrusted actor since the function is `onlyOwner`, but the broken check means the owner can release an NFT that is not in `ManagedNFTs`, and the contract will still emit an event and transfer the NFT out, potentially confusing off-chain accounting. Excluded from attacker-only scope but noted as a state-consistency defect.
hypotheses.impact: Inconsistent state between `ManagedNFTs` and actual ownership; misleading events.
hypotheses.recommendation: Replace with `require(found, "unable to find released NFT in ManagedNFTs");` using a boolean flag set in the loop.

hypotheses.title: _beforeTokenTransfer pushes address(0) into holders on burn
hypotheses.description: When `to == address(0)` (burn), the code skips the allowlist check but still executes `bool exists = (this.balanceOf(to) != 0); if (!exists) holders.push(to);`, pushing `address(0)` into `holders`. `_afterTokenTransfer` then tries to remove `from`, but `address(0)` remains in the array. Subsequent distributions iterate over `holders` and call `isApprovedHolder(address(0))` (false) so it is skipped, but the array grows with zero-address entries and `distributeToAllHolders` may run out of gas.
hypotheses.attackPath: Any approved holder can call `burn(amount)` (or `burnFrom`) to burn their entire balance, causing `address(0)` to be pushed into `holders`. Repeated burns by multiple holders bloat the array with zero addresses, increasing gas costs for all future distributions and potentially causing `distributeToAllHolders` to exceed the block gas limit.
hypotheses.impact: Denial of service / gas griefing on distributions; holders array corruption; potential inability to complete distributions.
hypotheses.recommendation: Only push `to` into `holders` when `to != address(0)`.

hypotheses.title: Missing chain ID and contract address in signed data (no signatures present)
hypotheses.description: The codebase does not implement any signature-based operations (no `permit`, no meta-transactions, no `ecrecover`). Therefore, there is no signed data to replay across chains or contracts. This finding is noted only to confirm the absence of signature-related vulnerabilities in the in-scope files.
hypotheses.attackPath: N/A — no signature verification exists to exploit.
hypotheses.impact: None.
hypotheses.recommendation: N/A.

hypotheses.title: Anyone can trigger distribution and lock all token transfers
hypotheses.description: `distribute()` is public with no access control. Any untrusted caller can invoke it once `MinDistributionPeriod` has elapsed, which calls `_beginDistribution()` and sets `LockedForDistribution = true`. This locks all transfers, mints, and burns until the entire distribution loop completes across all holders.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Wait until `block.number - LastDistribution >= MinDistributionPeriod`. 2. Call `distribute(1)` with a single distribution. 3. `_beginDistribution()` sets `LockedForDistribution = true`. 4. All `_beforeTokenTransfer` calls now revert with "distribution in progress". 5. Attacker can repeat this to keep the token locked, or grief by forcing a distribution at an inconvenient time.
hypotheses.impact: All token transfers, mints, and burns are frozen until someone completes the full distribution (which may be gas-prohibitive with many holders). Holders cannot move tokens; owner cannot mint. Denial of service on core token functionality.
hypotheses.recommendation: Restrict `distribute()` to `onlyOwner`, or allow anyone to call but ensure the lock cannot be triggered adversarially (e.g., only owner can begin a distribution).

hypotheses.title: Entitlement rounding leaves dust stranded in contract
hypotheses.description: `erc20EntitlementPerUnit[j] = balance / supply` truncates the per-unit entitlement. When multiplied back by each holder's balance, the sum of payouts is strictly less than `balance` whenever `balance % supply != 0`. The remainder is never distributed and accumulates in the contract, effectively being donated to future distributions (or locked if supply changes).
hypotheses.attackPath: An untrusted holder can deliberately keep a tiny balance (e.g. 1 wei) so that `balance % supply` is maximized relative to their share, or simply observe that after each distribution the contract retains `balance % supply` of each token. Over many distributions the stranded dust grows; a subsequent holder who mints right before a distribution can capture a disproportionate share of the accumulated dust relative to their contribution.
hypotheses.impact: Permanent accounting drift between contract token balances and sum of holder entitlements; dust is effectively lost to holders and can be captured asymmetrically by late minters.
hypotheses.recommendation: Track a per-token remainder and carry it forward, or distribute the remainder to the last recipient, or use a cumulative-reward-per-share accumulator (e.g. `rewardPerTokenStored`) so no dust is stranded.

hypotheses.title: distribute() ignores failed transfers and still marks recipient as paid
hypotheses.description: The loop calls `toDistribute.transfer(recipient, entitlement)` and only records the receipt if it returns true, but regardless of success it advances `nextDistributionRecipient` and eventually calls `_endDistribution()`. If a token's `transfer` returns false (e.g., a non-reverting ERC20 that returns false, or a blacklisted recipient), the recipient is silently skipped and the entitlement is lost, while the distribution is considered complete.
hypotheses.attackPath: An untrusted actor who is an approved holder and is blacklisted by a distributable ERC20 (or a token that returns false on transfer) can cause their own entitlement to be silently dropped; more importantly, any holder can be affected if a distributable token is a non-reverting false-returning token. The attacker cannot be prevented from being included, and the distribution completes without paying them, leaving funds stranded.
hypotheses.impact: Holders permanently lose their share of distributable tokens; contract retains funds that should have been paid out; distribution accounting is wrong.
hypotheses.recommendation: Revert on failed transfer (use SafeERC20 or require the return value), or skip and retry the recipient in a later distribution without advancing the index.

hypotheses.title: Anyone can trigger withdrawal from managed NFTs, griefing distribution
hypotheses.description: `withdrawFromManagedNFTs()` and `withdrawFromAllManagedNFTs()` are public with no access control. Any untrusted caller can force withdrawals from managed NFTs into the ERC20 contract at any time (when not locked). This changes the contract's ERC20 balances mid-cycle and can be used to manipulate the entitlement calculation or grief the owner.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker calls `withdrawFromManagedNFTs(ManagedNFTs.length)` at an arbitrary time. 2. All NFT balances are pulled into the ERC20 contract. 3. If a distribution is later started, the entitlement per unit is computed on these balances. 4. Attacker can also front-run the owner's intended withdrawal timing, or cause `nextWithdrawal` state to be manipulated.
hypotheses.impact: Unauthorized state changes to managed NFT balances; potential manipulation of distribution entitlements; griefing of protocol operations. No direct theft but loss of control over fund flow timing.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add `onlyOwner` to `withdrawFromManagedNFTs()` and `withdrawFromAllManagedNFTs()`.

hypotheses.title: First-depositor / donation attack inflates entitlement per unit
hypotheses.description: `entitlement = balance / supply` uses the contract's raw ERC20 balance, which can be inflated by anyone transferring tokens directly to the contract (donation) before the first distribution. If supply is small (e.g. 1 wei minted to attacker), the attacker's entitlement per unit becomes enormous, and they can drain the donated amount plus any subsequent deposits.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker is approved holder and gets 1 wei minted (or is the first minter). 2) Attacker (or any external actor) transfers a large amount of a distributable ERC20 directly to the contract. 3) Attacker calls `distribute()`; `entitlement = balance / 1 = balance`, so attacker receives the entire donated balance. 4) Any later minters receive nothing for that token until new revenue arrives.
hypotheses.impact: Theft of donated/accrued revenue from future holders; the attacker captures funds intended for the pool.
hypotheses.recommendation: Track internally-accounted balances per distributable token (incremented only via `withdrawFromManagedNFTs`) and compute entitlement from that tracked balance, not `IERC20.balanceOf(address(this))`.

hypotheses.title: Holder list grows unboundedly via zero-balance re-adds
hypotheses.description: `_beforeTokenTransfer` pushes `to` onto `holders` whenever `balanceOf(to) == 0` at the time of the transfer. Because `_afterTokenTransfer` only removes a holder when their balance becomes exactly zero, an attacker can repeatedly transfer 1 wei to themselves (or between approved accounts) to re-add themselves after each removal, or add many approved accounts. `distributeToAllHolders` and `distribute` iterate over `holders`, so a large list causes out-of-gas and blocks distributions.
hypotheses.attackPath: An approved holder with a tiny balance transfers all tokens away (removing themselves from `holders`), then receives 1 wei back (re-adding themselves). Repeating this across many approved accounts (or via `mintAndDistribute` if owner is tricked) inflates `holders.length`. When `distributeToAllHolders` is called, the loop exceeds block gas limit and reverts, preventing distributions and thus preventing mints/burns (which require a recent distribution).
hypotheses.impact: Denial of service on distributions, which in turn blocks minting and burning (via `_beforeMintOrBurn`), effectively freezing the protocol's supply management.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use an enumerable set with deduplication, or only add to `holders` on mint (from == address(0)) and remove on burn (to == address(0)), rather than on every zero-balance transition.

hypotheses.title: Distribution entitlement computed from live balance, allowing dilution via transfer
hypotheses.description: `_beginDistribution()` snapshots `erc20EntitlementPerUnit = balance / supply` at the start, but the per-recipient payout in `distribute()` multiplies that entitlement by `this.balanceOf(recipient)` at the time each recipient is processed. Because transfers are only blocked while `LockedForDistribution` is true, and the loop processes holders incrementally across multiple calls, a holder can move tokens between addresses (or to a fresh approved holder) between `distribute()` calls to double-count the same entitlement. The entitlement is fixed but the balance used to multiply it is not, so the same underlying tokens can be claimed more than once.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker holds X tokens and is in `holders`. 2) Owner/anyone calls `distribute(1)` which locks and pays the first holder. 3) Attacker transfers their X tokens to a second approved address that is later in the `holders` array (transfer is allowed because `LockedForDistribution` only blocks during the loop, and the attacker's own address may already have been processed). 4) When the loop reaches the second address, it pays `entitlement * X` again. 5) Repeat with additional approved addresses to drain the contract's distributable balances.
hypotheses.impact: Distributable ERC20 balances are drained to a single attacker, leaving other holders unpaid and the contract insolvent relative to entitlements.
hypotheses.recommendation: Snapshot each holder's balance at `_beginDistribution()` (e.g., store per-holder balances or use a checkpoint) and pay based on the snapshot, not on live `balanceOf` during the loop.

hypotheses.title: _afterTokenTransfer removes wrong holder due to missing break
hypotheses.description: The loop removing `from` from `holders` does not `break` after finding and removing the element. After swapping in the last element and popping, the loop continues iterating with a now-shorter array, potentially skipping elements or reading stale indices, and can remove additional unintended entries if duplicates exist.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker arranges for duplicate entries in `holders` (e.g., via the address(0) bug or transfer patterns). 2. On a transfer that zeroes a balance, the loop removes one entry but continues, potentially removing another holder's entry. 3. That holder is silently dropped from future distributions.
hypotheses.impact: Holders can be incorrectly removed from the distribution list, causing them to miss reward payouts (loss of yield).
hypotheses.recommendation: Add `break;` after the swap-and-pop in `_afterTokenTransfer`.

hypotheses.title: Fee-on-transfer / rebasing tokens break entitlement accounting
hypotheses.description: The contract assumes `IERC20(distributableERC20s[i]).balanceOf(address(this))` equals the sum of amounts actually received from managed NFTs. For fee-on-transfer tokens, the received amount is less than the withdrawn amount; for rebasing tokens, the balance changes over time. Entitlement is computed from the live balance, so holders may be over- or under-paid relative to what was actually earned, and the contract may attempt to transfer more than it holds.
hypotheses.attackPath: If a fee-on-transfer token is added to `distributableERC20s`, an untrusted actor can trigger `withdrawFromManagedNFTs` (public) to pull balances in, then call `distribute`. The entitlement math uses the post-fee balance, but the NFT's `_withdrawBalancesTo` already recorded the pre-fee amount in events; more importantly, if the token rebases downward between `_beginDistribution` and the transfer loop, `toDistribute.transfer` fails and the distribution stalls, locking the contract (`LockedForDistribution = true`) and freezing all transfers/mints/burns.
hypotheses.impact: Distribution can revert mid-loop, leaving `LockedForDistribution = true` and permanently freezing token transfers, mints, and burns until the owner intervenes; holders may receive incorrect amounts.
hypotheses.recommendation: Measure actual received amounts (balance delta) when withdrawing from NFTs and store them; disallow fee-on-transfer/rebasing tokens in `setDistributableERC20s`, or handle transfer failures by skipping rather than reverting.

hypotheses.title: Distribution can be permanently bricked by a disapproved holder
hypotheses.description: `distribute()` iterates over `holders` and only advances `nextDistributionRecipient` past entries it processes. If a holder is disapproved via `disapproveHolder()`, the loop still increments `i` and skips the transfer, so that is fine. However, the real issue is that `_beforeTokenTransfer` pushes `to` into `holders` whenever `balanceOf(to) == 0`, and `_afterTokenTransfer` removes `from` only when balance hits zero. A disapproved holder who still holds tokens remains in `holders` and is skipped, but the loop still terminates. The actual bricking vector: `distributeToAllHolders()` calls `distribute(holders.length)`, and if any single holder's ERC20 transfer reverts (e.g., a blacklisting token in `distributableERC20s`), the entire distribution reverts, leaving `LockedForDistribution = true` forever since `_endDistribution()` is never reached.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker gets added to `distributableERC20s` indirectly? No — owner controls that. Instead: attacker is an approved holder who receives a token that is later blacklisted by the ERC20 issuer (e.g., USDC blacklist). 2. Owner calls `distribute()`. 3. The `toDistribute.transfer(recipient, entitlement)` reverts for the blacklisted recipient. 4. `LockedForDistribution` stays true, blocking all transfers, mints, and burns. 5. No recovery function exists to unlock.
hypotheses.impact: All token transfers, mints, and burns are permanently frozen; funds in the contract are stuck; holders cannot exit.
hypotheses.recommendation: Wrap the per-recipient transfer in a try/catch or use a pull-based claim pattern, and add an owner-callable emergency unlock that resets `LockedForDistribution` without requiring full distribution.

hypotheses.title: Silent failure of ERC20 transfer in distribute() loses holder rewards
hypotheses.description: In `distribute()`, the code calls `toDistribute.transfer(recipient, entitlement)` and only records the receipt if the call returns true. If the transfer returns false (e.g., a non-standard ERC20 or a token that reverts on failure without bubbling), the loop continues without reverting, and `nextDistributionRecipient` advances. The holder permanently loses their entitlement for that distribution because `_endDistribution()` deletes `erc20EntitlementPerUnit` and resets state.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker deploys or causes a distributable ERC20 to be added that returns false on transfer (e.g., a token with a blacklist or a paused token). 2) Attacker ensures they are a holder. 3) When `distribute()` runs, the transfer to the attacker (or to others) returns false, the receipt is zero, but the distribution still completes. 4) The attacker's entitlement is lost and cannot be reclaimed.
hypotheses.impact: Permanent loss of holder rewards; funds remain stuck in the contract and are not redistributed.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use `SafeERC20.safeTransfer` and revert on failure, or explicitly handle failed transfers by not advancing the recipient index.

hypotheses.title: Entitlement rounding leaves dust that later holders can drain
hypotheses.description: `erc20EntitlementPerUnit` is computed as `balance / supply` (integer division), so the per-unit entitlement is truncated. The remainder (up to `supply - 1` wei per token) is never distributed and stays in the contract. On the next distribution, that leftover is included in the new `balance`, so it is redistributed to whoever holds tokens at that time rather than to the holders who were entitled to it.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker holds tokens during distribution N, receiving truncated entitlements. 2) After distribution N ends, attacker acquires (or is minted) tokens before distribution N+1. 3) The dust from distribution N is folded into the balance used for distribution N+1, and the attacker claims a share of it despite not having been a holder when it accrued. 4) Repeat across many distributions to accumulate rounding dust.
hypotheses.impact: Systematic leakage of undistributed rewards to later holders; earlier holders are underpaid and the attacker captures value they did not earn.
hypotheses.recommendation: Track undistributed remainders per token and carry them forward explicitly, or distribute the remainder proportionally (e.g., allocate dust to the last recipient) so it is not re-awarded to future holders.

hypotheses.title: burnFromAndDistribute allows burning others' tokens without allowance check bypass
hypotheses.description: `burnFromAndDistribute()` is public and calls `burnFrom(account, amount)`, which internally checks allowance via `_spendAllowance`. However, the function first calls `distributeToAllHolders()` if the period has elapsed, which locks the contract. If the distribution completes, `burnFrom` then executes. The concern is that any caller can trigger a distribution (locking the contract) as a side effect of attempting to burn, even if they have no allowance — the distribution side effect happens before the allowance check reverts.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker calls `burnFromAndDistribute(victim, 1)` with no allowance. 2. If `_isPastMinDistributionPeriod()`, `distributeToAllHolders()` runs and locks the contract. 3. `burnFrom` then reverts on allowance. 4. Net effect: attacker forced a distribution/lock without authorization.
hypotheses.impact: Griefing — attacker can force distributions and lock the token at will by calling this function with any account/amount, even without allowance.
hypotheses.recommendation: Check allowance before triggering distribution, or restrict distribution triggering to owner.

hypotheses.title: `_afterTokenTransfer` removal loop can leave duplicate holders
hypotheses.description: The removal loop iterates over `holders` and, upon finding `from`, swaps in the last element and pops, but does not `break`. After the swap, the element now at index `i` is the former last element, which is then re-checked; if it equals `from` (duplicate entry), it is removed again, but if the loop continues past a match without break, it can also skip or mis-handle duplicates. More critically, if `from` appears multiple times (possible because `_beforeTokenTransfer` pushes on every zero-balance transition without dedup), only one instance is removed per call, leaving stale entries that are still iterated during distribution.
hypotheses.attackPath: An attacker who is an approved holder can create duplicate entries in `holders` by transferring their entire balance away and back (each zero-balance transition pushes them again). When they later transfer away, only one duplicate is removed, leaving a stale entry. During `distribute`, the stale entry is iterated; `isApprovedHolder` may still be true, and `balanceOf(recipient)` is 0, so `entitlement = 0` and a zero-value transfer is attempted (or skipped), wasting gas and potentially causing the distribution to stall if the token reverts on zero transfers.
hypotheses.impact: Gas waste and potential distribution stall; holder list drifts from reality, breaking the invariant that `holders` contains exactly the current holders.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add `break` after removal and deduplicate on insertion; better, maintain a mapping of holder index and only add/remove on mint/burn.

hypotheses.title: Entitlement truncation leaves dust and can be gamed via supply changes
hypotheses.description: `entitlement = balance / supply` truncates integer division, so `entitlement * supply < balance` and the remainder stays in the contract. Because `_endDistribution()` deletes `erc20EntitlementPerUnit` and `LastDistribution` is reset, the leftover dust accumulates and is never attributed to holders. A holder who is the sole holder at distribution time captures the full balance, but with multiple holders the truncation systematically underpays.
hypotheses.attackPath: An attacker who controls the timing of distributions (via `mintAndDistribute`/`burnAndDistribute` being callable by anyone for burn variants) can arrange to be the only holder at distribution time, capturing the entire balance, then re-add other holders afterward. Alternatively, repeated small distributions let the attacker capture rounding remainders that should belong to others.
hypotheses.impact: Systematic underpayment of holders and accumulation of stranded funds in the contract; a timing attacker can capture rounding remainders.
hypotheses.recommendation: Track and carry forward the undistributed remainder, or distribute the remainder to the last recipient, rather than discarding it.

hypotheses.title: Disapproved holder with balance blocks distribution completion
hypotheses.description: When a holder is disapproved via `disapproveHolder()`, they remain in the `holders` array as long as they hold a balance. In `distribute()`, the `if (isApprovedHolder(recipient))` check skips them, but `nextDistributionRecipient` still advances past them, so this alone does not block. However, `_beforeTokenTransfer` requires `isApprovedHolder(to)`, so a disapproved holder cannot transfer their tokens away, and `_afterTokenTransfer` only removes them from `holders` when their balance reaches zero. Since they can never transfer out, they are permanently stuck in `holders`. This is not a DoS by itself, but combined with the fact that `distributeToAllHolders()` is called by `mintAndDistribute`/`burnAndDistribute`, a disapproved holder with balance causes those convenience functions to iterate over them harmlessly. The real DoS: if `holders.length` grows large (each new recipient with zero balance is pushed), `distributeToAllHolders()` will exceed block gas limit.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker (approved holder) transfers tiny amounts to many fresh approved addresses (or the owner approves many). 2. Each transfer to a zero-balance address pushes to `holders`. 3. `holders` grows unbounded. 4. `distributeToAllHolders()` and `mintAndDistribute()`/`burnAndDistribute()` revert with out-of-gas. 5. `LockedForDistribution` may be set true by a partial `distribute()` call, then the loop cannot complete.
hypotheses.impact: Distribution and mint/burn convenience functions become uncallable; if `LockedForDistribution` is set, all transfers freeze.
hypotheses.recommendation: Cap `holders` growth, use a pull-based distribution, or allow `distribute()` to be called in bounded chunks without requiring full completion in one tx (already partially supported, but `distributeToAllHolders` should not be used in mint/burn paths).

hypotheses.title: releaseManagedNFT silently fails to remove NFT from array
hypotheses.description: `releaseManagedNFT()` transfers the NFT out and then loops over `ManagedNFTs` to remove it. If the NFT is not found (e.g., it was already released or never added), the loop completes without removing anything, and the `require(true, ...)` is a no-op that always passes. The NFT is transferred out but remains in `ManagedNFTs`, so `withdrawFromManagedNFTs()` will later call `withdrawBalancesTo` on an NFT this contract no longer owns, which will revert (access control), bricking withdrawals.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Owner calls `releaseManagedNFT` for an NFT that is in `ManagedNFTs`. 2. The NFT is transferred out and removed. 3. Later, owner calls `releaseManagedNFT` again for the same NFT (or a duplicate address was added). 4. The transfer reverts because the contract no longer owns it — actually the transfer would revert first. The real issue: if `ManagedNFTs` contains a duplicate entry, the loop removes only the first occurrence, leaving a stale entry. 5. `withdrawFromManagedNFTs()` iterates and calls `withdrawBalancesTo` on the stale entry, which reverts (not owner), bricking the entire withdrawal loop.
hypotheses.impact: Withdrawals from managed NFTs become permanently blocked; funds in remaining NFTs are stuck.
hypotheses.recommendation: Replace `require(true, ...)` with a real check that the NFT was found and removed, and prevent duplicate entries in `addManagedNFT`.

hypotheses.title: Distribution entitlement uses stale balance causing over/under payment
hypotheses.description: `_beginDistribution()` snapshots `erc20EntitlementPerUnit` based on the supply at the start of the distribution, but `distribute()` pays each recipient `entitlement * this.balanceOf(recipient)` at the time of the loop iteration. Because transfers are locked during distribution, balances cannot change mid-distribution, but the entitlement is computed against the full contract balance of each distributable ERC20 while the loop pays out per-holder sequentially. If a holder is skipped (not approved) or the loop is split across multiple calls, the remaining balance is not re-snapshotted, so later recipients can be paid from a pool that has already been partially drained, or the last recipients receive less than their entitlement.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker becomes an approved holder with a small balance. 2) Attacker triggers `distribute()` in small increments so that early recipients drain the ERC20 balance. 3) When the attacker's turn arrives, the contract may have insufficient balance for the computed entitlement, causing `transfer` to fail silently (the `if (toDistribute.transfer(...))` swallows failures) and the attacker's receipt is recorded as zero while the entitlement was already "spent" conceptually. 4) Alternatively, if the attacker is the last recipient, they receive the residual balance which may be larger than their fair share if earlier transfers failed.
hypotheses.impact: Incorrect reward distribution; some holders receive less than owed, others may receive more; funds can be stranded in the contract if transfers fail silently.
hypotheses.recommendation: Recompute entitlement per unit after each transfer, or revert on failed transfers and track remaining balance explicitly; do not silently ignore `transfer` return values.

hypotheses.title: withdrawBalancesTo allows approved spender to redirect funds
hypotheses.description: `withdrawBalancesTo()` allows any approved operator (via `_isApprovedOrOwner`) to specify an arbitrary `destination` address. An approved spender can therefore redirect all ERC20 balances held by the NFT to any address, including their own, without the owner's consent. This is a form of unauthorized fund redirection enabled by the approval mechanism.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker gets approved as an operator for the AccountId (e.g., via `setApprovalForAll` or `approve`). 2) Attacker calls `withdrawBalancesTo(erc20s, attackerAddress)`. 3) All balances are transferred to the attacker.
hypotheses.impact: Loss of all ERC20 balances held by the NFT.
hypotheses.recommendation: Restrict `withdrawBalancesTo` to the owner only, or require the destination to be the owner unless explicitly authorized.

hypotheses.title: Holder can be paid twice via duplicate entries in holders array
hypotheses.description: `_beforeTokenTransfer` pushes `to` onto `holders` whenever `balanceOf(to) == 0` at the time of the transfer. Because the check is performed before the balance is updated, a transfer that sends the full balance away and then receives it back (or a mint to a zero-balance account) can re-add an address that is already present in `holders`. The `distribute` loop iterates over `holders` and pays each entry, so a duplicated address is paid multiple times for the same entitlement.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker is an approved holder with a balance. 2) Attacker transfers their entire balance to another approved account (or burns), making `balanceOf(attacker) == 0`; `_afterTokenTransfer` removes them from `holders`. 3) Attacker receives tokens again (transfer or mint), and `_beforeTokenTransfer` pushes them back onto `holders`. 4) If the removal loop in `_afterTokenTransfer` fails to find/remove the entry (e.g., due to the swap-and-pop skipping the moved element), the address remains and is pushed again, creating a duplicate. 5) During `distribute`, the attacker is paid once per duplicate entry.
hypotheses.impact: Attacker drains more than their fair share of distributable ERC20s, leaving other holders underpaid and potentially emptying the contract's reward balance.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use a mapping to track membership in `holders` and only push when the address is not already present; fix the removal loop to iterate correctly after swap-and-pop.

hypotheses.title: Entitlement computed on full balance but transfers can fail silently
hypotheses.description: In `distribute`, `entitlement` is computed from `erc20EntitlementPerUnit[j] * balanceOf(recipient)`, but the transfer is only recorded in `receipts` if `toDistribute.transfer` returns true. If a token's transfer returns false (e.g., a non-standard ERC20 or a token that blocks transfers), the entitlement is silently skipped and the loop continues. The contract does not revert or adjust accounting, so the distribution completes with `_endDistribution` and `LastDistribution` updated, permanently losing that portion of rewards for that cycle.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker (or a malicious/blocking token added via `setDistributableERC20s` by owner — but attacker can also be a holder of a token that reverts on transfer to certain addresses) causes `transfer` to return false for a recipient. 2) The distribution loop skips the entitlement without reverting. 3) `_endDistribution` is called, resetting entitlements and updating `LastDistribution`. 4) The skipped funds remain in the contract and are folded into the next distribution, benefiting future holders instead of the intended recipient.
hypotheses.impact: Holders are silently underpaid; funds are redistributed to later holders or stuck, breaking fair distribution.
hypotheses.recommendation: Revert on failed transfers or track failed entitlements and carry them forward; do not finalize the distribution if any transfer fails.

hypotheses.title: _afterTokenTransfer removes only first matching holder, leaving duplicates
hypotheses.description: The loop removes the first occurrence of `from` in `holders` but does not `break` after removal, and the swap-and-pop pattern can leave duplicate entries if `from` appears multiple times (which can happen because `_beforeTokenTransfer` pushes `to` whenever `balanceOf(to) == 0`, including when `to` already exists in the array from a prior zero-balance state). Duplicates cause the same holder to be paid multiple times in a distribution.
hypotheses.attackPath: An approved holder can transfer their entire balance away (triggering removal) and then receive tokens again (triggering a push), potentially creating duplicate entries. During `distribute`, the same recipient is iterated multiple times and receives multiple entitlements, draining the contract's distributable balances faster than intended.
hypotheses.impact: Over-distribution to a single holder, insolvency for other holders, incorrect accounting.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use a mapping to track holder membership and ensure uniqueness; break after removal.

hypotheses.title: `distribute` skips unapproved holders but still advances index, losing their share
hypotheses.description: In the distribution loop, if `isApprovedHolder(recipient)` is false, the recipient's entitlement is silently skipped and `nextDistributionRecipient` advances past them. The skipped entitlement remains in the contract and is not redistributed to other holders in the same distribution (entitlement per unit was already fixed). A holder who is disapproved after `_beginDistribution` but before their turn loses their share permanently to the contract.
hypotheses.attackPath: An untrusted actor cannot directly disapprove others (owner-only), but a holder can be disapproved by the owner at any time. More relevantly, an attacker who is an approved holder can front-run their own disapproval (if they anticipate it) by calling `distribute` themselves to ensure they are processed while still approved; conversely, if the owner disapproves a holder mid-distribution, that holder's share is stranded. The untrusted angle: any holder can call `distribute` and choose `numDistributions` to control which recipients are processed, potentially ensuring a disapproved holder is skipped and their share remains locked.
hypotheses.impact: Entitlements are permanently stranded in the contract when a holder is disapproved mid-distribution; the accounting no longer matches the intended per-unit payout.
hypotheses.recommendation: Either require all holders to be approved at `_beginDistribution` time, or accumulate skipped entitlements into a remainder pool for the next distribution.

hypotheses.title: burnAndDistribute/burnFromAndDistribute allow burning before distribution completes
hypotheses.description: `burnAndDistribute` calls `distributeToAllHolders()` only if `_isPastMinDistributionPeriod()`. If a distribution is already in progress (`LockedForDistribution == true`) but `_isPastMinDistributionPeriod()` returns false (e.g., because `LastDistribution` was just updated or supply/holders conditions), the burn proceeds. More importantly, `distributeToAllHolders()` may revert on gas if there are many holders, and the burn is then skipped — but if it succeeds partially, `LockedForDistribution` remains true and the subsequent `burn` reverts, leaving state inconsistent. The check does not verify `LockedForDistribution` before attempting the burn path.
hypotheses.attackPath: A holder calls `burnAndDistribute` when a distribution is mid-flight. If `_isPastMinDistributionPeriod()` is false, `distributeToAllHolders` is skipped and `burn` executes while `LockedForDistribution` is true — but `_beforeTokenTransfer` requires `!LockedForDistribution`, so it reverts. The real exploit is that a holder can call `burnAndDistribute` to force a full distribution attempt that reverts on gas, griefing other holders' ability to complete distributions.
hypotheses.impact: Griefing / denial of service on distribution completion; holders unable to burn or complete distributions.
hypotheses.recommendation: Explicitly check `!LockedForDistribution` and handle partial distributions, or require the caller to complete the distribution before burning.

hypotheses.title: Reentrancy in distribute() via malicious ERC20 transfer callback
hypotheses.description: The distribute() function iterates over holders and calls IERC20.transfer(recipient, entitlement) before updating nextDistributionRecipient. A malicious ERC20 in distributableERC20s (set by owner, but the token contract itself is untrusted code) can reenter distribute() or other functions during the transfer callback. Since nextDistributionRecipient is only updated after the loop, a reentrant call would re-process the same recipients, draining the contract's token balances multiple times.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker deploys a malicious ERC20 that calls back into LiquidInfrastructureERC20.distribute() on transfer(). 2) Owner adds it to distributableERC20s (or it's already present). 3) During a distribution, when the malicious token's transfer() is invoked for a recipient, it reenters distribute() with numDistributions>0. 4) Because nextDistributionRecipient hasn't been advanced yet, the same recipients are paid again from the contract's balance. 5) Repeat until contract balance is drained.
hypotheses.impact: Contract's ERC20 balances drained; other holders receive nothing; accounting (erc20EntitlementPerUnit) becomes meaningless.
hypotheses.recommendation: Update nextDistributionRecipient before performing transfers, or use a pull-based claim pattern, or add a reentrancy guard that also covers the transfer loop (nonReentrant is present but the malicious token can still reenter via a different path if any exists — verify all entry points).

hypotheses.title: Reentrancy in withdrawFromManagedNFTs via malicious NFT contract
hypotheses.description: withdrawFromManagedNFTs() calls withdrawFrom.getThresholds() and withdrawFrom.withdrawBalancesTo(...) on each ManagedNFT. A malicious ManagedNFT (added by owner, but the NFT contract code is untrusted) can reenter withdrawFromManagedNFTs() or other functions. nextWithdrawal is only updated after the loop, so a reentrant call restarts from the same index, and the malicious NFT can also reenter distribute() or mint/burn paths. The function lacks nonReentrant.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker controls a LiquidInfrastructureNFT-like contract added to ManagedNFTs. 2) Its withdrawBalancesTo() reenters withdrawFromManagedNFTs() (or distribute()) before nextWithdrawal is updated. 3) The same NFT is processed repeatedly, or state is corrupted. 4) Combined with a malicious ERC20, funds can be siphoned.
hypotheses.impact: Repeated withdrawals, state corruption of nextWithdrawal, potential fund loss.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add nonReentrant to withdrawFromManagedNFTs and update nextWithdrawal before external calls.

hypotheses.title: Zero-amount transfer reverts block distribution
hypotheses.description: In `distribute()`, `toDistribute.transfer(recipient, entitlement)` is called even when `entitlement == 0` (e.g., when `erc20EntitlementPerUnit[j]` is zero because the contract's balance of that token is less than total supply). Some ERC20 tokens (e.g., certain non-standard or paused tokens) revert on zero-value transfers. If any token in `distributableERC20s` reverts on zero transfer, the entire distribution reverts, and `LockedForDistribution` remains true.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Owner adds a token to `distributableERC20s` that reverts on zero transfer (or the token's balance is zero so entitlement is zero). 2. `distribute()` is called. 3. Transfer of 0 reverts. 4. `LockedForDistribution` stays true, freezing all transfers/mints/burns.
hypotheses.impact: Permanent freeze of the token contract; funds stuck.
hypotheses.recommendation: Skip transfers when `entitlement == 0`, and wrap transfers in try/catch.

hypotheses.title: withdrawFromManagedNFTs reverts on any single NFT failure
hypotheses.description: `withdrawFromManagedNFTs()` loops over `ManagedNFTs` and calls `withdrawFrom.withdrawBalancesTo(withdrawERC20s, address(this))`. If any single NFT's `withdrawBalancesTo` reverts (e.g., a token in its thresholds reverts on transfer, or the NFT was released but not removed from the array), the entire loop reverts. Since `nextWithdrawal` is only updated after the loop, a single bad NFT blocks all withdrawals from all subsequent NFTs.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker (or owner) adds an NFT whose `getThresholds()` returns a token that reverts on transfer (e.g., a malicious ERC20). 2. `withdrawFromManagedNFTs()` is called. 3. The malicious token's transfer reverts. 4. The entire withdrawal loop reverts, and `nextWithdrawal` is not advanced. 5. All other NFTs' funds are stuck.
hypotheses.impact: Funds in all managed NFTs are permanently stuck; withdrawals cannot proceed.
hypotheses.recommendation: Wrap each NFT's withdrawal in try/catch and advance `nextWithdrawal` regardless of individual failures.

hypotheses.title: Withdrawal from ManagedNFTs can be front-run to dilute distribution
hypotheses.description: `withdrawFromManagedNFTs` is callable by anyone and pulls balances from ManagedNFTs into the contract. If called just before a distribution, the withdrawn funds are included in the distribution balance and shared among current holders. An attacker who is about to become a holder (or who can acquire tokens cheaply before the distribution) can front-run the withdrawal, acquire tokens, and then claim a share of the newly withdrawn rewards without having held during the period the rewards accrued.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes pending rewards in ManagedNFTs. 2) Attacker acquires tokens (if approved) or arranges to be an approved holder before the withdrawal. 3) Attacker calls `withdrawFromManagedNFTs` (or lets someone else call it) to move funds into the contract. 4) Attacker ensures a distribution occurs while they hold tokens, claiming a share of rewards that accrued before they joined.
hypotheses.impact: Rewards are redistributed to latecomers, diluting long-term holders and enabling reward sniping.
hypotheses.recommendation: Separate reward accrual from withdrawal timing, or require a holding period before new holders can claim distributions; alternatively, snapshot entitlements based on balances at the time rewards were earned.

hypotheses.title: withdrawFromManagedNFTs uses stale thresholds and can revert on empty list
hypotheses.description: The function calls `withdrawFrom.getThresholds()` and passes the returned ERC20 list to `withdrawBalancesTo`. If a managed NFT has an empty threshold list (or thresholds changed to exclude a token that actually holds a balance), those balances are never withdrawn. Additionally, `withdrawBalancesTo` requires `_isApprovedOrOwner(_msgSender(), AccountId)`; since `msg.sender` is the LiquidInfrastructureERC20 contract and it owns the NFT, this works, but if ownership was transferred out without removal from `ManagedNFTs`, the call reverts and blocks the entire withdrawal loop.
hypotheses.attackPath: An untrusted actor cannot directly call this (it's public but operates on managed NFTs owned by the contract). However, if a managed NFT's ownership is transferred away (e.g., via a separate path) the loop reverts, and any caller of `withdrawFromManagedNFTs` is blocked. Also, tokens held by the NFT but not in its threshold list are permanently stranded.
hypotheses.impact: Frozen funds in managed NFTs; denial of service on withdrawals.
hypotheses.recommendation: Iterate over `distributableERC20s` (or a superset) rather than only thresholds, and handle per-NFT failures gracefully.

hypotheses.title: withdrawFromManagedNFTs uses NFT thresholds as token list, ignoring actual balances
hypotheses.description: The function reads `withdrawFrom.getThresholds()` and passes only those ERC20 addresses to `withdrawBalancesTo`. If the NFT holds balances in tokens not currently in its threshold list (e.g., thresholds were changed after revenue accrued, or revenue arrived in a token never added to thresholds), those balances are never withdrawn and remain stuck in the NFT. The contract's distributable balance therefore under-reports actual assets, and `_beginDistribution` computes entitlements on an incomplete balance.
hypotheses.attackPath: An attacker (or any party able to influence threshold changes on a managed NFT, e.g., via the NFT owner if it is not this contract) can cause revenue tokens to be excluded from thresholds, so `withdrawFromManagedNFTs` skips them. Distributions then compute entitlements on a smaller balance, and the excluded tokens are permanently stranded in the NFT.
hypotheses.impact: Under-distribution to holders and permanently stranded funds in managed NFTs; incorrect entitlement accounting.
hypotheses.recommendation: Withdraw all tokens the NFT actually holds (or maintain an authoritative token list) rather than relying solely on current thresholds.

hypotheses.title: No slippage/minimum-out protection on distribution transfers
hypotheses.description: `distribute()` transfers a computed `entitlement` amount to each recipient with no minimum-out or slippage parameter. If a distributable token is fee-on-transfer or otherwise non-standard, the recipient may receive less than the computed entitlement while the contract's accounting assumes the full amount was paid. There is no check that the recipient's balance increased by the expected amount.
hypotheses.attackPath: If a fee-on-transfer token is added to `distributableERC20s` (by owner, but the token itself is untrusted), each distribution silently loses value to the token's fee mechanism, and the contract's internal accounting (which assumes full transfer) diverges from reality. A malicious token could also re-enter or manipulate balances.
hypotheses.impact: Holders receive less than entitled; accounting mismatch between computed entitlements and actual balances.
hypotheses.recommendation: Measure balance delta before/after transfer and use the actual received amount, or restrict distributable tokens to standard ERC20s.

hypotheses.title: Read-only reentrancy via balanceOf during distribution entitlement calc
hypotheses.description: _beginDistribution() reads IERC20(distributableERC20s[i]).balanceOf(address(this)) to compute entitlements. If any distributable token is a malicious contract, its balanceOf can be manipulated or can reenter during the read (though view functions can't reenter state-changing calls directly, they can be used by external protocols reading this contract's state mid-distribution). More critically, LockedForDistribution is set true but external protocols reading totalSupply/balanceOf during the distribution window see inconsistent state.
hypotheses.attackPath: An external protocol integrating with this ERC20 reads balanceOf/entitlement state while LockedForDistribution is true and nextDistributionRecipient is partially advanced, leading to incorrect pricing or share calculations in the integrating protocol.
hypotheses.impact: Integrators misprice shares; potential arbitrage against protocols relying on this token's state.
hypotheses.recommendation: Document and enforce that integrations must check LockedForDistribution; consider exposing a view that reverts during distribution.

hypotheses.title: burnAndDistribute / burnFromAndDistribute reentrancy via distributeToAllHolders
hypotheses.description: burnAndDistribute() calls distributeToAllHolders() (which is not nonReentrant itself but calls distribute() which is) and then burn(). If distribute() reverts or if a malicious token reenters during distribute's transfer loop, the burn may execute against stale state. More importantly, burnFromAndDistribute allows an approved spender to trigger a distribution and then burnFrom, and the distribution's external transfers can reenter burnFromAndDistribute.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker with an approved allowance calls burnFromAndDistribute; during the distribute() transfer loop a malicious token reenters burnFromAndDistribute, causing double-burn or burning more than intended.
hypotheses.impact: Unauthorized or excessive burning of victim's tokens.
hypotheses.recommendation: Wrap burnAndDistribute/burnFromAndDistribute in nonReentrant and ensure distribute completes before burn.

hypotheses.title: _beforeTokenTransfer holder push allows duplicate entries via reentrancy
hypotheses.description: _beforeTokenTransfer pushes `to` onto holders if balanceOf(to)==0. During a distribution, LockedForDistribution blocks transfers, but mint/burn paths and the distribute loop's external transfers can interleave. If a recipient's balance is drained to zero by a malicious token mid-loop and then re-credited, duplicate holder entries can be created, causing double distributions.
hypotheses.attackPath: Malicious ERC20 in distributableERC20s manipulates balances during transfer so that a holder's balance hits zero and is re-added, duplicating them in holders[].
hypotheses.impact: Duplicate distributions, inflated entitlements, fund drain.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use a mapping-based holder set instead of an array, or guard holder insertion with a flag.

hypotheses.title: releaseManagedNFT external call before state update enables reentrancy
hypotheses.description: releaseManagedNFT() calls nft.transferFrom(address(this), to, nft.AccountId()) before removing the NFT from ManagedNFTs. A malicious NFT contract (ERC721 with overridden transferFrom or a hook) can reenter releaseManagedNFT or withdrawFromManagedNFTs during the transfer, before the ManagedNFTs array is updated. nonReentrant is present, but the malicious NFT can reenter other non-guarded functions like withdrawFromManagedNFTs.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker's malicious NFT reenters withdrawFromManagedNFTs() during transferFrom, causing the NFT to be withdrawn from while still in ManagedNFTs, or reenters addManagedNFT to duplicate entries.
hypotheses.impact: Duplicate ManagedNFT entries, repeated withdrawals, state corruption.
hypotheses.recommendation: Remove the NFT from ManagedNFTs before calling transferFrom, or add nonReentrant to withdrawFromManagedNFTs.

hypotheses.title: recoverAccount() emits event without on-chain verification of recovery
hypotheses.description: `recoverAccount()` only emits a `TryRecover` event and relies on the off-chain x/microtx module to detect it and transfer all balances to the NFT. There is no on-chain confirmation or nonce to prevent replay of the recovery event, and no deadline. If the off-chain module processes the event multiple times (e.g., due to a reorg or replay), the account could be drained repeatedly or the recovery could be triggered without the owner's intent if the event is spoofed.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes a `TryRecover` event. 2) If the off-chain module does not deduplicate events, the attacker can cause the recovery to be processed multiple times, draining the account. 3) Alternatively, if the event is not authenticated, an attacker could emit a similar event from a different contract to trick the module.
hypotheses.impact: Potential repeated draining of the Liquid Account; loss of funds.
hypotheses.recommendation: Include a nonce and chain ID in the event, and have the off-chain module verify the event source and deduplicate.

hypotheses.title: Minting after distribution period can dilute pending rewards
hypotheses.description: `mintAndDistribute` calls `distributeToAllHolders()` only if `_isPastMinDistributionPeriod()` is true, then mints. However, `mint` itself is gated by `_beforeMintOrBurn` which requires `!_isPastMinDistributionPeriod()`. If the period has elapsed, `distributeToAllHolders` runs and resets `LastDistribution`, allowing the mint. But if `distributeToAllHolders` fails (e.g., out of gas due to many holders), the mint reverts. More importantly, the owner can mint right after a distribution, diluting the entitlement per unit for the next cycle without the new holder having contributed to the rewards already in the contract. Since `_beginDistribution` uses the current supply, a large mint between distributions reduces each existing holder's share of the already-accumulated balance.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Rewards accumulate in the contract from ManagedNFTs. 2) Owner (trusted) mints a large amount to an approved account before the next distribution. 3) The new supply dilutes `erc20EntitlementPerUnit`, so existing holders receive less than the rewards they were entitled to. While the owner is trusted, the same effect can be triggered by any approved holder who receives a mint, and the timing is exploitable by the recipient.
hypotheses.impact: Existing holders are diluted; rewards accrued before the mint are partially captured by the new holder.
hypotheses.recommendation: Snapshot supply at the time rewards accrue, or require that minting only occurs immediately after a distribution and before new rewards are withdrawn, with explicit accounting for pre-mint balances.
